## Summary of findings

**CRITICAL — Authentication bypass via JKU injection** (`src/oauth/token.js`, `src/oauth/jwks.js`)
`verifyExternalToken` trusts the attacker-controlled JWT `jku` header to fetch the verification key. The only guard is a `startsWith('https://keys.example.test')` prefix check, bypassable via `https://keys.example.test.evil.com/...` or `https://keys.example.test@evil.com/...`. An attacker hosts their own JWKS, signs a token with their key, and the verifier accepts the forged token → full auth bypass. The unused `src/http/safe-jwks.js` shows the correct, hardcoded approach.

**CRITICAL — Open redirect / authorization-code theft** (`src/oauth/register.js`, `src/oauth/client-repo.js`)
`validateRedirect` uses `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)`, bypassable via `https://portal.example.test.evil.com/cb` or `https://portal.example.test@evil.com/cb`. This lets an attacker receive OAuth codes/credentials meant for the legitimate client. An exact-match helper (`exact-redirect.js`) exists but is not used.

**LOW — Unhandled error on unregistered client** (`src/oauth/register.js`, `src/oauth/client-repo.js`)
`byId` returns `undefined` for unknown clients; `validateRedirect` then throws a `TypeError` reading `.baseUrl`, instead of cleanly denying.

Files reviewed but clean: `config.js` (RS256 only), `state.js` (timing-safe, length-checked state comparison), `pkce.js` (standard S256 challenge), `safe-jwks.js` (correct decoy, unused), `logging.js`, `exact-redirect.js`. No dependency metadata (e.g., `package.json`) exists in the repo.
